rows: This method is the most suitable for determining the density of transparent liquid petroleum products.

Place part of the sample in the density cylinder, immerse a thermometer in it, and make sure that the temperature of both the sample and the cylinder is the standard temperature at which the density is to be determined (this temperature is specified according to the specifications to which the liquid is subject).
Select the hydrometer suitable for this method, immerse it in the sample and leave it to settle, floating in the sample.
At the standard temperature, take the hydrometer reading.
If the standard temperature is not the temperature at which the sample density is to be measured, the density value can be corrected by calculation.
It is the mass of a unit volume of the liquid at the standard temperature (15°C, 20°C); the unit of density is kg/m³ (kg/m3).
Density
The sample is taken in the correct manner mentioned above, in accordance with MPIS (Oil-013-r2).
Make sure the data on the sample are correct.
Make sure the sample is placed in its own box so that it is not exposed to sunlight and dust.
Make sure the sample bottle is dry (free of water and dust).
When carrying out the test, avoid spilling oil on the floor; if this happens, remove it.
Glass hydrometers graduated in density units, conforming to specification IEC 296-82.
Thermometers with a clear graduation range (error within the permissible limits).

A water bath with a constant temperature (if available) that can hold the hydrometer cylinder containing the hydrometer and the sample; the rate of change of the water bath temperature does not exceed 0.25°C from the standard temperature.
Transfer the sample to a clean cylinder whose inside diameter is 25 mm larger than the outside diameter of the hydrometer, without spilling any drops of the sample, to avoid forming air bubbles.
Remove any air bubbles formed on the surfaces by lightly touching them with filter paper, before immersing the hydrometer.

Make sure the cylinder is in a completely vertical position, away from air currents, taking care that the ambient temperature does not change by more than 2°C during the whole test period; if this is not observed, use a water bath that maintains the cylinder temperature throughout the test period.

Immerse the suitable thermometer and stir the sample with a rod in a vertical circular motion to ensure a stable temperature distribution, then record the sample temperature to the nearest 0.1°C, then remove the thermometer and the stirring rod from the cylinder.
Note: when the thermometer is used as a means of measuring temperature, it can also be used as a stirring rod.

Place the suitable hydrometer in the sample so that the distance between the end of the hydrometer and the bottom of the cylinder is 25 mm, and leave it for a suitable time to settle and for air bubbles to rise to the surface and be removed before taking any hydrometer reading. When the hydrometer is floating freely in the sample, away from the cylinder walls, record the hydrometer reading to the nearest 0.2.
The hydrometer reading is recorded from the point where the observer eye meets the liquid surface level on the hydrometer scale, as shown in the attached figure.

Immerse the thermometer again in the cylinder, stir vertically, then lift the hydrometer out of the sample and record the temperature to the nearest 0.1°C. If the measured temperature differs from that measured previously by more than 0.5°C, the temperature must be readjusted to the nearest 0.5°C; if this is not possible, use a water bath with a constant temperature and repeat the measurement in the same way again.
Note: the measured density is most accurate when the measurement temperature is closest to the standard temperature.
Correct the temperature values for the thermometer used and average the two readings to the nearest 0.1°C.
Correct the reading values of the hydrometer scale used to the nearest 0.1 kg/m³.

If the temperature at measurement is not adjusted to the nearest 0.5°C, the density value is corrected using the following relation: r20 = rT {1 + X(T - 20)} where r20 is the density at 20°C (assuming the standard temperature for this liquid is 20°C), rT is the density measured at T, and X (the correction factor) = a × 10⁻⁵·65.

sections_target.text: Precision: Precision is subject to laboratory results as follows:

rows: Repeatability: the difference between two results for the same person, the same apparatus, the same operating conditions and the same material at the same temperature is 0.5 kg/m³.
Reproducibility: the difference between two results for two different persons for the same sample at the same temperature is 1.2 kg/m³.

Introduction
This method is used to determine the density of petroleum products at a specific standard temperature (usually 15°C or 20°C), noting that this density can be estimated at another temperature and the value then corrected to the standard temperature by calculation.
This document was prepared by the chemist Ghada Soliman Ahmed Mohamed, reviewed by the chemist Abdel Nasser Mohamed El-Amin, tested by the chemist Ashraf Salah El-Din Saleh, and approved by the chemist Mohamed Wagdy Abdallah, General Manager of High Dam Power Station, Hydro Power Plants Company for Electricity Production, and certified by Eng. This document is approved by Eng. Mohamed Osama Soliman Selim, MPIS Coordinator, Hydro Power Plants Company for Electricity Production.
Objective
This method is the most suitable for determining the density of transparent liquid petroleum products.
Summary of Method
Place part of the sample in the density cylinder, immerse a thermometer in it, and make sure that the temperature of both the sample and the cylinder is the standard temperature at which the density is to be determined (this temperature is specified according to the specifications to which the liquid is subject). |

At the standard temperature, take the hydrometer reading. | 
If the standard temperature is not the temperature at which the sample density is to be measured, the density value can be corrected by calculation. | 
Definition
It is the mass of a unit volume of the liquid at the standard temperature (15°C, 20°C); the unit of density is kg/m³ (kg/m3). | Density

Procedures to be Carried Out
Test Steps
Transfer the sample to a clean cylinder whose inside diameter is 25 mm larger than the outside diameter of the hydrometer, without spilling any drops of the sample, to avoid forming air bubbles. | 1.

Immerse the thermometer again in the cylinder, stir vertically, then lift the hydrometer out of the sample and record the temperature to the nearest 0.1°C. Calculations
